name: Kela
catalog_quote: Stress is not emic, as a consistent pattern was found to explain its occurrence. In one, two, and three syllable words, the stress is on the first syllable. One exception was found: /awe/ [a'we] 'yesterday' /awe/ ['awe] 'lizard'. Where the word has more than three syllables, the stress is on the third last syllable. audit.recode_to: Drop 'fixed-strict antepenult' (counts as exceptionless (the strict set), antepenultimate stress). reclassify as non-strict/variable right-edge stress: penult default (obligatory in disyllables), antepenult in a lexically specified subset of 3+-syllable words, with inter-speaker and phrasal variation (Ransdell-Green 2022 sec. 2.5 pp.36-38, sec. 3.4 pp.64-66, sec. 4.5 pp.109-110, Southern Kala); keep Collier & Collier 1975 pp.149-150 as the Apoze-dialect statement (initial in 1-3 sigma, antepenult in 4+ sigma) in a dialect/caution note. Deciding source should become Ransdell-Green 2022; strength of the evidence rises (dissertation with duration measurement) while 'strict' and 'dom' flags fall.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Collier 1975 passage is present verbatim in the held scanned at printed pp.149-150 (PDF pp.21-22), sec. 3.3.1. (2) Deciding source is a 1975 SIL 'tentative phonemic statement' of one northern dialect; the best available description is Ransdell-Green's 2022 UH Manoa phonology dissertation (Glottolog's top-ranked ref, 245 pp), which we already hold but which the stress record ignores. Read at sec. 2.5/3.4/4.5 it describes penult-tending stress, always penult in disyllables, antepenult 'in some cases' for 3+-syllable words (lexical: /ˈguɾuwa/ vs /guɾuˈwaɾa/, /gaˈɾawe/, /soˈɾome/~/ˈsoɾome/), plus speaker and phrasal variation -- incompatible with a strict, exceptionless antepenult rule; Collier's own 4-5-syllable transcriptions are likewise mixed. (3) Only one un-held primary item exists (Johnson 1994 Kui OPD, 4 pp); it could not be downloaded (SIL an automated-access block, IA outag
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again: confirmed in the copy we hold. I re-opened lines 659-681 and rendered the scan itself (PDF pp.21-22 = printed pp.149-150) to PNG and read the page images: sec. 3.3.1 'Tone, Stress, and Length' carries verbatim 'Stress is not emic, as a consistent pattern was found to explain its occurrence. In one, two, and three syllable words, the stress is on the first syllable. One exception was found: /awe/ [a'we] 'yesterday' /awe/ ['awe] 'lizard'. Where the word has more than three syllables, the stress is on the third last syllable.' and p.150 'There are predictable exceptions to this rule.
